# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- site-visual-check: Screenshot and visually verify site/ (claudinite.com), desktop and mobile, and deliver the result to the owner. Use when changing site/ markup, CSS, or animations, or when checking responsive/mobile rendering.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). # Extract lessons from repo activity

what reading *artifacts* adds.

## Capture at the repo's own level

Write each lesson at whatever level reads naturally for this repo — refer to its files, services, or
mechanics wherever that's what makes the lesson clear. Don't force either extreme: don't contort a lesson
to be hyper-specific, and don't polish it into a general, portable rule. Making a lesson portable is the
growth lifecycle's **promote** stage, done canon-side later over whatever merged here; here, just capture

## Read the window — and read merged PRs properly

Work only the window you were handed (a scheduled run gets it as binding scope in the work item's

   review discussion. A merged PR is usually the window's richest lesson source, because it records what
   was tried, what a reviewer pushed back on, and why the landed shape won. A verdict reached in review

*reason* is not obvious from the code; a review comment that names a convention the author missed; a

logs that actually carry the timestamps.

the repo's own voice.

rule that cannot be made confident lands as prose instead — never as a broken check.

adding nothing.

1	# Delivering a scheduled task's pull request
2	
3	How an executor subagent delivers the PR its task produced — the AGENT lane of the one
4	delivery procedure. The CODE lane is `land-pr.mjs` beside this file (Action-side workers
5	run it); **the two must keep saying the same thing** — a nuance changed in one changes in
6	the other in the same commit. Your GitHub writes go through the session's MCP tools, and
7	your pushes ride a credential whose events start workflows normally, so — unlike the code
8	lane — your PR's checks need no help from you to run.
9	
10	## The task sets the ceiling; the repo decides the rest
11	
12	Your task's declared `expected_outcome` is a **ceiling, not a plan**:
13	
14	- **`open-pr`** — open the PR and stop. Never arm auto-merge, never merge. Nothing below
15	  applies to you.
16	- **`merged-pr`** — the task *may* land its PR. Whether it actually lands unreviewed is
17	  **this repo's** setting, read in step 1 — never the task's own knowledge. The same task
18	  lands itself on one repo and waits for an owner on another, and both are correct.
19	
20	## 1. Read the repo's delivery preference
21	
22	`.claudinite-settings.json` → `maintenance.delivery`:
23	
24	- **`auto-merge`** (legacy aliases `auto`, `push`) — go to step 2.
25	- **`review`** (legacy alias `pr`) — leave the PR open for the owner and stop. Never arm
26	  it, never merge it, and never read the standing PR as a failure: degrading `merged-pr`
27	  to open-pr is the repo's stated intent, and member config wins.
28	- **Missing or empty** — proceed as `auto-merge` (the default). Do **not** write the key:
29	  materializing it is the update converge's job, not yours.
30	- **Anything else** — someone stated an intent you cannot honour, and guessing could
31	  deliver its opposite. Leave the PR open (the posture that merges nothing) and name the
32	  unrecognized value in your wrap-up comment on the work item.
33	
34	## 2. Arm auto-merge
35	
36	Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
37	it once this repo's required checks pass.
38	
39	## 3. When the arm is rejected
40	
41	- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
42	  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
43	  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
44	  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
45	  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
46	- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
47	  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
48	  PR's **head sha**:
49	  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
50	    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
51	  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
52	    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
53	  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
54	    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
55	    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
56	    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
57	    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
58	    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
59	    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the `merged-pr` ceiling — the trail
60	    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
61	    unseen check does not survive anything.
62	
63	## Never
64	
65	Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
66	arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
67	manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
68	are always legal outcomes.

1	# claudinite-growth
2	
3	Opt into the **growth lifecycle** — declaring this pack enrolls a repo in contributing its hard-won
4	lessons up to the shared Claudinite canon, and in pruning its local packs once the canon owns them.
5	Seeded by default (`--init` + the one-time `grow-with-claudinite-seed` baseline migration for the
6	existing fleet), and **opt-out by removal**: baselining never re-adds it.
7	
8	This pack carries the **repo-side** stages of the growth lifecycle: capturing a repo's own
9	lessons into its local packs, and pruning them once the shared canon covers them. The central
10	**promote** stage — which lifts portable lessons up into the shared canon — is a home-only duty
11	that runs canon-side, not a repo-side task, so it lives outside this pack.
12	
13	Its scheduled work is five tasks under this pack's own `tasks/`, each discovered by the repo's
14	scheduler (`engine/scheduler/discover.mjs`) wherever the pack is declared:
15	
16	| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
17	|---|---|---|
18	| `growth-extract` ([tasks/growth-extract/task.md](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) | the project changed in the window | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI |
19	| `growth-dedup` ([tasks/growth-dedup/task.md](tasks/growth-dedup/task.md)) | weekly, when the canon or the project's local packs moved in the week | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI |
20	| `growth-discover-packs` ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) | weekly | a new **local** pack in the repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`, via a reviewed PR |
21	| `prose-to-checks-sweep` ([tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md](tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)) | weekly (no-ops cheaply on a quiet corpus) | a PR converting always-testable pack prose into checks |
22	| `rule-revalidation` ([tasks/rule-revalidation/task.md](tasks/rule-revalidation/task.md)) | weekly | a reviewed PR correcting rules whose environment claim no longer probes true |
23	
24	(Plus two agentless tasks over the conversation-logs branch: [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/README.md) hourly,
25	described below, and `logs-prune` — retention, [tasks/logs-prune/worker.mjs](tasks/logs-prune/worker.mjs).)
26	
27	## Extraction is one task over two sources
28	
29	`growth-extract` is the whole capture stage, and it runs **three skills** in order:
30	
31	1. [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) over the window's commits, merged
32	   PRs and issue discussion;
33	2. [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) over the logs captured
34	   from working sessions;
35	3. [prose-to-checks](skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) over the prose **that run just wrote**, to see
36	   whether any of it upgrades to a check before the PR opens.
37	
38	Everything lands in **one** PR, delivered to land where the repo's delivery settings allow
39	(`engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md`). The two extraction halves used to be two tasks firing in
40	the same nightly anchor against the same local packs; they share the lesson bar, the promotion ladder
41	and the dedup surface ([extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md)), so the split bought nothing
42	and cost a second opus dispatch, a second PR, and two runs deduping against a corpus the other was
43	concurrently writing.
44	
45	The third step is why the standing `prose-to-checks-sweep` is **weekly**: fresh prose is already
46	offered a conversion the night it is written, so what the sweep sees is a backlog that moves on a
47	weekly clock.
48	
49	A member that wants the local stages without contributing lessons upstream **opts out of
50	promotion** on its own entry — `{ "id": "claudinite-growth", "config": { "promote": false } }`
51	— and the central promote stage skips it (absent or `true` = participate).
52	
53	## The conversation lifecycle — capture in-session, extract in the daily task, retention
54	
55	The pack also owns **extraction from working sessions**, replacing the old in-session post-merge
56	lessons pass. Capture and extraction split by what each needs: **capture** needs the live session

59	scheduled task — the logs branch is *in the repo*, so reading it, committing lessons to local packs,
60	and pruning are plain local git on the working tree; only posting the summary on the issue uses the
61	GitHub MCP tools.

63	1. **Capture — a step in the merge-to-main skill** (in-session, where the transcript lives).
64	   Right after a merge lands:
65	   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
66	   (in the canon repo itself: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`).
67	   Deterministic, seconds; it bundles the session transcript (sidechains inline, timestamp
68	   order), **scrubs enumeration-first** (every value the environment holds — `process.env`
69	   minus a short named allowlist of structural values, plus known credential stores — is
70	   redacted wherever it appears, with credential-shape patterns as the backstop; a secret the
71	   session itself transformed is beyond any static scrub, and push protection is the last
72	   net), and pushes one file per **capture event** onto the orphan **`conversation-logs`**
73	   branch: `<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`, commits marked `[skip ci]`.
74	   **Delta-aware, keyed on the session id:** every capture pushes only the entries after this
75	   session's previous capture, whatever event produced it, so any two events chain into
76	   disjoint files and a zero delta pushes nothing at all. Double-writing is therefore safe by
77	   construction, not by coordination — the property [`session-end.mjs`](session-end.mjs) relies
78	   on, so `test/pack.test.mjs` pins it directly.
79	   The branch is a **work queue, not an archive** — never merged; tips are cheap in shallow
80	   session clones and retention keeps them bounded.
81	1. **Capture — again, when the session ends** ([session-end.mjs](session-end.mjs), invoked by the
82	   engine's SessionEnd hook runner for every active pack that ships one). Same capture, with
83	   `--issue 0`: **`0` means "no associated issue"**, and the filename shape stays byte-identical
84	   on purpose — the retention prune, the `conversationLogs` signal and the extract's filename
85	   parse all already accept it, whereas a *new* shape would be invisible to the prune and become
86	   immortal on the branch. This event is what captures the sessions that never merge (a review, an
87	   investigation, a session that ended in a question) and the post-merge **tail** of the ones that
88	   do. **Best effort:** a container reclaimed by timeout never fires it, so nothing depends on it
89	   having run — every firing enriches the record, every miss leaves exactly the merge-only
90	   behaviour. An `issue-0` log has no issue for the extract to post its exchange
91	   summary on; nothing else about its lifecycle differs.
92	   **Unattended sessions capture through the same step, deliberately not through the hook.** A
93	   scheduled task's executor session ends by having its container reclaimed, which is exactly
94	   the ending no `SessionEnd` fires on — so the executor runs the engine's runner itself as its
95	   last step and names its work item in `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE`, which this step uses in
96	   place of `0`. Those logs therefore file under the task that ran (the item's title
97	   names `pack/task`), and the work no human watched becomes as countable as the work one did.

99	   (precondition: a substantive merge; local git on the repo's working tree, MCP only for the issue comment). It
100	   applies the [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) skill (the
101	   friction signals and the measured efficiency analysis, computable from the log's timestamps and
102	   token usage) over [extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md)'s shared bar, routes keepers into
103	   the member's local packs, and posts on the worked issue, for each rule that landed, a
104	   **200-word-max** summary of the slice of conversation that caused it — the dialogue itself is
105	   never pasted there, it is far too verbose for an issue —
106	   **extraction is the only path to permanence**: a log that yields no rule gets no comment,
107	   and its conversation is gone once retention deletes it (a deliberate owner call).
108	3. **Deletion — the agentless `logs-prune` task**
109	   ([tasks/logs-prune/worker.mjs](tasks/logs-prune/worker.mjs)), daily, over the same branch: every
110	   capture past `config.retention_days` is removed, on the stamp in its filename alone. What makes
111	   that safe without an agent is the reading window above — the extract run reads from the oldest end
112	   of the branch on every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. **Unset retention = the
113	   prune deletes nothing** (capture-only, fail-safe).
114	
115	No adoption question over it — `retention_days` stays unset (hidden) by default, which is
116	fail-safe (capture-only). A project that wants the prune active sets `config.retention_days`
117	itself (10 is the recommended floor); nothing else to schedule, since both tasks ride the
118	fleet's one daily run like the other growth tasks.
119	
120	## Skill-usage metrics — what the mounted skills actually do
121	
122	Mounting a skill only puts its name and one-line description into the session prompt; whether the
123	model ever **loads** it is discretion, and nothing recorded it. So the promotion ladder's
124	skill-vs-prose call had no empirical feedback: a skill whose trigger never fires looked exactly like
125	one that fires daily, and a "skill" that loads in every session (rules wearing a skill's clothes)
126	looked exactly like a genuinely activity-scoped one.
127	
128	The [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/README.md) task closes that loop — hourly, agentless, seconds. It
129	counts skill loads **and their denominators** (captures, merges, sessions, user messages, user
130	commands) out of the logs this pack already captures, into
131	`.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`: day rows recomputed statelessly inside the raw retention
132	window, week rows appended once past a `foldedThrough` watermark. Denominators are the point — a raw
133	count cannot tell healthy-rare from broken, so the question is loads *against the sessions where that
134	skill's own declared trigger plausibly applied*. Zeros are implicit (a skill with no loads has no
135	key), which is what makes "never loads" visible: diff the file against the repo's mounted skills.
136	
137	Fleet-wide aggregation is deliberately **not** here — the canon knows mechanisms, never repos, so
138	it belongs to the fleet-enforcer repo, the only place that knows who the members are.
139	
140	## Skills
141	
142	Each stage's **method** lives in a skill, so the task doc frames the unattended run and the same
143	method is available to an owner asking in-session. Extract's three are listed above;
144	[**growth-dedup**](skills/growth-dedup/SKILL.md) is the dedup stage's — what to prune, strip, or
145	rephrase, the keep-test, and the shrink-only discipline. The pack also bundles
146	[unattended-agents](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md),
147	[generate-project-instructions](skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) and
148	[**writing-tasks**](skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md) — the contract a `tasks/<name>/task.mjs` and
149	its worker are written to: the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the
150	precondition as the only place a task may decide not to run, and how a work item converges. That
151	contract is what the four task checks below judge against, and it is a skill rather than a rule
152	because it is wanted when a task is being written, not carried by every session in every repo.
153	Adoption itself — `adopt-claudinite`, `adopt-pack` and the `adopt-requested-packs` task — is not
154	here: its subject is Claudinite's own surface, not lesson capture.
155	
156	## Rules (`RULES.md`)
157	
158	| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
159	|---|---|---|---|
160	| Changing a local pack automatically | high | complexity | prose: 65 words |
161	| Wanting a job to run in Actions | high | complexity | prose: 55 words + check (`scheduler-workflow-shape`) |
162	
163	## Coded rules
164	
165	| Rule | Kind | What |
166	|---|---|---|
167	| `dedup-prune-integrity` | work-scope ([dedup-integrity.mjs](workRules/dedup-integrity.mjs)) | a dedup edit only removes portable text — never grows a local pack or re-imports a canon rule |
168	| `growth-write-scope` | work-scope ([growth-write-scope.mjs](workRules/growth-write-scope.mjs)) | a capture run (extract, dedup) writes only the repo's own local packs |
169	
170	The capture runs' write surface is the local packs and nothing else — a run improves the repo's
171	**packs**, never the canon it prunes against or the project's own code. `growth-write-scope` is
172	the machine guarantee behind that, keyed on the pinned commit titles of exactly those two runs; the
173	lifecycle's wider-surfaced runs have their own gates (promote writes the canon under `packs/` and
174	`skills/`, certified by canon-curation's `promote-scope`; pack discovery also writes the repo-root
175	declaration that activates the pack it authors).
176	
177	**Pack discovery** ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) is
178	an ordinary weekly task on the repo's own scheduler. The repo runs the whole pipeline over
179	**itself**: manifest its stack, hold it against the canon packs already on its shelf and its own
180	existing local packs, and — for genuinely project-specific knowledge neither homes — author a new
181	**local** pack populated from its real usage, landed through a **reviewed** PR (a new pack ships new
182	`.mjs` checks, and a check can break CI — the same reason `prose-to-checks-sweep` is reviewed, and
183	the one place this stage differs from extract). It writes only the repo's own
184	`.claudinite/local/packs/`; lifting a local pack up into the shared canon is the central promote
185	task's job.
186	
187	## Rules expire when the environment moves — revalidation
188	
189	Capture, dedup and conversion all assume a rule is either right or superseded. A third failure mode
190	has no local signal at all: the rule was right, and the **world** changed. A claim that the harness
191	rejects a call in some shape, that the Action's token cannot push a path, that an MCP tool exists —
192	each is a fact about a platform this repo does not control, and when it stops being true nothing
193	here goes red. The prose keeps reading as authoritative, sessions keep obeying it, and the cost
194	lands as a session spent on a route that closed.
195	
196	[rule-revalidation](tasks/rule-revalidation/task.md) is the weekly re-probe. It takes **every**
197	environment-dependent claim in the capture surface — the judgment prose that makes up most of a pack
198	is out of scope, so that set is far smaller than the corpus — **runs** the smallest read-only thing
199	that would distinguish true from false for each, and corrects what the probe contradicts, in a
200	reviewed PR whose body carries the probe evidence, since that is the one thing a reviewer cannot
201	re-derive from the diff. Its scope is the same `pack_paths` config `prose-to-checks-sweep` reads, so
202	a repo names its capture surface once. Covering the whole set every run is what lets the task hold
203	no state between runs: there is no "what did I probe last time" to remember.
204	
205	The dangerous verdict is the one it refuses to reach. An executor session carries the reach its
206	repo's routine was provisioned with, which is not the reach every rule was written under, so a probe
207	that cannot run is logged **unprobed** and the rule is left untouched. Rewriting a rule into "you
208	cannot do X" because one session could not is unfalsifiable afterwards and removes the capability
209	from every future session — which is why an unprobed
210	claim is reported in the run's PR body as explicitly as a corrected one.
211	
212	## Identifying a project's capture surface: its local packs (the same way in every stage)
213	
214	Every growth stage operates on a project's **local packs** — the tracked packs a repo keeps under
215	`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` (prose in `RULES.md`, checks in the pack's `rules`, activity
216	procedures as the pack's skills, scheduled tasks under its `tasks/`). That subtree **is** the
217	project's own content;
218	the rest of `.claudinite/` is the **read-only mounted canon** and is never a capture, prune, or
219	promote target. So "a project's local packs" means precisely *everything under
220	`.claudinite/local_packs/`, and nothing else under `.claudinite/`*. This is the normalized capture
221	surface — a structural set the stages read the same way, not a `CLAUDE.md`-graph walk over stray
222	Markdown (a repo with no local packs yet simply has nothing to extract, dedup, or promote here; a
223	project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill).
224	
225	Prefer the strongest mechanism the lesson allows — the **local promotion ladder**, applied at the
226	project's own level: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** whose failure message carries the lesson —
227	a **declared** one in the owning pack's `declared-checks.json` wherever patterns over files can say it,
228	a **rule module** in its `rules` only where they can't — an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack
229	skill**, and only what none of those can carry lands as **prose** in a pack's `RULES.md`. A check relieves every session's
230	context completely where prose only relocates it, so capture writes *more checks and less prose*.
231	
232	The stages differ only in *how they read that set*, never in *which set it is*: extract and dedup
233	run against the member repo and read the local packs from the working tree; promote runs centrally
234	and reads the same subtree over the GitHub API (get-file-contents under `.claudinite/local_packs/`).
235	Extract writes into it, promote reads from it, dedup prunes within it — all against the identical,
236	`.claudinite/local_packs/`-rooted set.
237	
238	## The change record: each local pack's own `VERSIONS.md`
239	
240	A canon pack's `VERSIONS.md` carries one row per version bump. A local pack is neither versioned nor
241	distributed, so its `VERSIONS.md` carries the same thing at the only granularity it has: **one row
242	per change automatic work made to it** — a prose rule added or removed, a check created, a rule
243	corrected against a probe or deleted as irrelevant.
244	
245	| Date | Task | Change |
246	|---|---|---|
247	| 2026-08-23 | `growth-extract` | Added: **Restoring source after a see-it-fail mutation** — `git checkout --`, never a `.bak`. |
248	| 2026-08-23 | `prose-to-checks-sweep` | Converted to a check: the entry-point await rule → `pack-discovery-entry-await`. |
249	
250	Every growth task writes its own rows, in the same PR as the change they describe, so the record
251	diffs beside what it records and travels with the pack it is about. A reader looking at a rule and
252	wondering where it came from is already in the directory.
253	
254	This is the growth lifecycle's **whole** record: no growth task keeps a standing tracker issue. An
255	issue body is rewritten in place with no history, sits outside the PR that made the change, and is
256	one sweep away from being closed as stale — none of which is true of a tracked file. A run that
257	changed nothing writes no row at all: the file logs what happened to the pack, never that a run
258	happened.
259	
260	`seedRepoLocalPack` creates the file empty at adoption, so no task has to invent it.
261	
262	## Checks
263	
264	| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
265	|---|---|---|---|
266	| `dedup-prune-integrity` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
267	| `growth-write-scope` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
268	| `in-session-github-access` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
269	| `routine-structure` | medium | complexity | check: blocking |
270	| `task-declaration-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
271	| `task-declaration-matches-folder` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
272	| `task-code-work-env` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
273	| `task-md-only-when-agentic` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
274	| `task-phase-discipline` | medium | complexity | check: advisory |
275	
276	The last five are the **task contract** ([the writing-tasks skill](skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md)), which
277	lives here because it judges whether a task is *written* correctly — authoring, the subject of this
278	pack — and not whether Claudinite is *working* in the repo. Relevance-first: all five are inert until
279	the repo carries a `tasks/<name>/task.mjs` of its own.
280	
281	- `task-declaration-shape` — a task declaration the scheduler reads is incomplete or illegal, so the task never fires or fires wrong.
282	- `task-declaration-matches-folder` — a declaration disagrees with its folder: discovery drops it into `errors` and every run keeps reporting healthy without it.
283	- `task-code-work-env` — a task reads a `CLAUDINITE_*` variable code-work never sets, so a parameter (a scope filter, a dry-run switch) silently never arrives and the run goes green in its most dangerous mode.
284	- `task-md-only-when-agentic` — an agentless task carries a `task.md`, which the corpus reads as "an agent runs here": prose no session will ever open, judged by the routine contract and named by every work item as the file the run is about.
285	- `task-phase-discipline` — a task decides not to run after its precondition already said run, hiding the decision from the run records.

lessons up to the shared Claudinite canon, and in pruning its local packs once the canon owns them.
Seeded by default (`--init` + the one-time `grow-with-claudinite-seed` baseline migration for the
existing fleet), and **opt-out by removal**: baselining never re-adds it.

This pack carries the **repo-side** stages of the growth lifecycle: capturing a repo's own
lessons into its local packs, and pruning them once the shared canon covers them. The central
**promote** stage — which lifts portable lessons up into the shared canon — is a home-only duty
that runs canon-side, not a repo-side task, so it lives outside this pack.

Its scheduled work is five tasks under this pack's own `tasks/`, each discovered by the repo's
scheduler (`engine/scheduler/discover.mjs`) wherever the pack is declared:

| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
|---|---|---|
| `growth-extract` ([tasks/growth-extract/task.md](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) | the project changed in the window | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI |
| `growth-dedup` ([tasks/growth-dedup/task.md](tasks/growth-dedup/task.md)) | weekly, when the canon or the project's local packs moved in the week | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI |
| `growth-discover-packs` ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) | weekly | a new **local** pack in the repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`, via a reviewed PR |
| `prose-to-checks-sweep` ([tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md](tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)) | weekly (no-ops cheaply on a quiet corpus) | a PR converting always-testable pack prose into checks |
| `rule-revalidation` ([tasks/rule-revalidation/task.md](tasks/rule-revalidation/task.md)) | weekly | a reviewed PR correcting rules whose environment claim no longer probes true |

(Plus two agentless tasks over the conversation-logs branch: [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/README.md) hourly,
described below, and `logs-prune` — retention, [tasks/logs-prune/worker.mjs](tasks/logs-prune/worker.mjs).)

3. [prose-to-checks](skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) over the prose **that run just wrote**, to see

and cost a second opus dispatch, a second PR, and two runs deduping against a corpus the other was
concurrently writing.

offered a conversion the night it is written, so what the sweep sees is a backlog that moves on a
weekly clock.

Each stage's **method** lives in a skill, so the task doc frames the unattended run and the same
method is available to an owner asking in-session. Extract's three are listed above;
[**growth-dedup**](skills/growth-dedup/SKILL.md) is the dedup stage's — what to prune, strip, or
rephrase, the keep-test, and the shrink-only discipline. The pack also bundles
[unattended-agents](skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md),
[generate-project-instructions](skills/generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md) and
[**writing-tasks**](skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md) — the contract a `tasks/<name>/task.mjs` and
its worker are written to: the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the
precondition as the only place a task may decide not to run, and how a work item converges. That
contract is what the four task checks below judge against, and it is a skill rather than a rule
because it is wanted when a task is being written, not carried by every session in every repo.
Adoption itself — `adopt-claudinite`, `adopt-pack` and the `adopt-requested-packs` task — is not
here: its subject is Claudinite's own surface, not lesson capture.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Changing a local pack automatically | high | complexity | prose: 65 words |
| Wanting a job to run in Actions | high | complexity | prose: 55 words + check (`scheduler-workflow-shape`) |

## Coded rules

| Rule | Kind | What |
|---|---|---|
| `dedup-prune-integrity` | work-scope ([dedup-integrity.mjs](workRules/dedup-integrity.mjs)) | a dedup edit only removes portable text — never grows a local pack or re-imports a canon rule |
| `growth-write-scope` | work-scope ([growth-write-scope.mjs](workRules/growth-write-scope.mjs)) | a capture run (extract, dedup) writes only the repo's own local packs |

The capture runs' write surface is the local packs and nothing else — a run improves the repo's
**packs**, never the canon it prunes against or the project's own code. `growth-write-scope` is
the machine guarantee behind that, keyed on the pinned commit titles of exactly those two runs; the
lifecycle's wider-surfaced runs have their own gates (promote writes the canon under `packs/` and
`skills/`, certified by canon-curation's `promote-scope`; pack discovery also writes the repo-root
declaration that activates the pack it authors).

**Pack discovery** ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) is
an ordinary weekly task on the repo's own scheduler. The repo runs the whole pipeline over
**itself**: manifest its stack, hold it against the canon packs already on its shelf and its own
existing local packs, and — for genuinely project-specific knowledge neither homes — author a new
**local** pack populated from its real usage, landed through a **reviewed** PR (a new pack ships new
`.mjs` checks, and a check can break CI — the same reason `prose-to-checks-sweep` is reviewed, and
the one place this stage differs from extract). It writes only the repo's own
`.claudinite/local/packs/`; lifting a local pack up into the shared canon is the central promote
task's job.

## Rules expire when the environment moves — revalidation

Capture, dedup and conversion all assume a rule is either right or superseded. A third failure mode
has no local signal at all: the rule was right, and the **world** changed. A claim that the harness
rejects a call in some shape, that the Action's token cannot push a path, that an MCP tool exists —
each is a fact about a platform this repo does not control, and when it stops being true nothing
here goes red. The prose keeps reading as authoritative, sessions keep obeying it, and the cost
lands as a session spent on a route that closed.

[rule-revalidation](tasks/rule-revalidation/task.md) is the weekly re-probe. It takes **every**
environment-dependent claim in the capture surface — the judgment prose that makes up most of a pack
is out of scope, so that set is far smaller than the corpus — **runs** the smallest read-only thing
that would distinguish true from false for each, and corrects what the probe contradicts, in a
reviewed PR whose body carries the probe evidence, since that is the one thing a reviewer cannot
re-derive from the diff. Its scope is the same `pack_paths` config `prose-to-checks-sweep` reads, so
a repo names its capture surface once. Covering the whole set every run is what lets the task hold
no state between runs: there is no "what did I probe last time" to remember.

The dangerous verdict is the one it refuses to reach. An executor session carries the reach its
repo's routine was provisioned with, which is not the reach every rule was written under, so a probe
that cannot run is logged **unprobed** and the rule is left untouched. Rewriting a rule into "you
cannot do X" because one session could not is unfalsifiable afterwards and removes the capability
from every future session — which is why an unprobed
claim is reported in the run's PR body as explicitly as a corrected one.

## Identifying a project's capture surface: its local packs (the same way in every stage)

Every growth stage operates on a project's **local packs** — the tracked packs a repo keeps under
`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` (prose in `RULES.md`, checks in the pack's `rules`, activity
procedures as the pack's skills, scheduled tasks under its `tasks/`). That subtree **is** the
project's own content;
the rest of `.claudinite/` is the **read-only mounted canon** and is never a capture, prune, or
promote target. So "a project's local packs" means precisely *everything under
`.claudinite/local_packs/`, and nothing else under `.claudinite/`*. This is the normalized capture
surface — a structural set the stages read the same way, not a `CLAUDE.md`-graph walk over stray
Markdown (a repo with no local packs yet simply has nothing to extract, dedup, or promote here; a
project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill).

Prefer the strongest mechanism the lesson allows — the **local promotion ladder**, applied at the
project's own level: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** whose failure message carries the lesson —
a **declared** one in the owning pack's `declared-checks.json` wherever patterns over files can say it,
a **rule module** in its `rules` only where they can't — an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack
skill**, and only what none of those can carry lands as **prose** in a pack's `RULES.md`. A check relieves every session's
context completely where prose only relocates it, so capture writes *more checks and less prose*.

The stages differ only in *how they read that set*, never in *which set it is*: extract and dedup
run against the member repo and read the local packs from the working tree; promote runs centrally
and reads the same subtree over the GitHub API (get-file-contents under `.claudinite/local_packs/`).
Extract writes into it, promote reads from it, dedup prunes within it — all against the identical,
`.claudinite/local_packs/`-rooted set.

## The change record: each local pack's own `VERSIONS.md`

A canon pack's `VERSIONS.md` carries one row per version bump. A local pack is neither versioned nor
distributed, so its `VERSIONS.md` carries the same thing at the only granularity it has: **one row
per change automatic work made to it** — a prose rule added or removed, a check created, a rule
corrected against a probe or deleted as irrelevant.

| Date | Task | Change |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-23 | `growth-extract` | Added: **Restoring source after a see-it-fail mutation** — `git checkout --`, never a `.bak`. |
| 2026-08-23 | `prose-to-checks-sweep` | Converted to a check: the entry-point await rule → `pack-discovery-entry-await`. |

Every growth task writes its own rows, in the same PR as the change they describe, so the record
diffs beside what it records and travels with the pack it is about. A reader looking at a rule and
wondering where it came from is already in the directory.

This is the growth lifecycle's **whole** record: no growth task keeps a standing tracker issue. An
issue body is rewritten in place with no history, sits outside the PR that made the change, and is
one sweep away from being closed as stale — none of which is true of a tracked file. A run that
changed nothing writes no row at all: the file logs what happened to the pack, never that a run
happened.

`seedRepoLocalPack` creates the file empty at adoption, so no task has to invent it.

## Checks

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dedup-prune-integrity` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `growth-write-scope` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `in-session-github-access` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `routine-structure` | medium | complexity | check: blocking |
| `task-declaration-shape` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-declaration-matches-folder` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-code-work-env` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-md-only-when-agentic` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `task-phase-discipline` | medium | complexity | check: advisory |

The last five are the **task contract** ([the writing-tasks skill](skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md)), which
lives here because it judges whether a task is *written* correctly — authoring, the subject of this
pack — and not whether Claudinite is *working* in the repo. Relevance-first: all five are inert until
the repo carries a `tasks/<name>/task.mjs` of its own.

- `task-declaration-shape` — a task declaration the scheduler reads is incomplete or illegal, so the task never fires or fires wrong.
- `task-declaration-matches-folder` — a declaration disagrees with its folder: discovery drops it into `errors` and every run keeps reporting healthy without it.
- `task-code-work-env` — a task reads a `CLAUDINITE_*` variable code-work never sets, so a parameter (a scope filter, a dry-run switch) silently never arrives and the run goes green in its most dangerous mode.
- `task-md-only-when-agentic` — an agentless task carries a `task.md`, which the corpus reads as "an agent runs here": prose no session will ever open, judged by the routine contract and named by every work item as the file the run is about.
- `task-phase-discipline` — a task decides not to run after its precondition already said run, hiding the decision from the run records.

  blow the MCP token limit — this repo's tracker issues (`Claudinite tracker:
  <dimension>`) accumulate long comment histories, so a bare title search returns

  `fields: ["number", "title", "state"]` (or similarly narrow) on the *first* call

  maximum allowed tokens" error forces a retry. Hit independently in three separate
  scheduled runs (issues #159, #161, #168), each paying a wasted round-trip (and,
  twice, a manual dump-and-reparse) for a result the narrowed call answers cleanly.

- **Never amend a subagent's already-pushed commit, and never relay a fabricated
  "fix" instruction for a check that doesn't exist as described, when a
  mid-dispatch Stop-hook finding turns out to be a background subagent's shared
  checkout misread as your own.** Issue #98: the orchestrator sent the subagent
  exactly such an instruction (which the subagent correctly refused as looking
  like an injection) and attempted `git commit --amend` on the subagent's
  already-pushed commit — blocked only by the permission classifier. **If the
  checkout-back or the amend is itself refused by the permission classifier,
  don't retry or force it** — a live subagent is using the shared checkout. Issue
  #116 hit exactly this: both remedies were blocked mid-run, and the orchestrator
  correctly left the branch untouched and waited; the branch reverted to the
  orchestrator's own assigned one, and the false-positive noise with it, the
  moment the subagent finished.

- **After a background subagent's handle goes unreachable following a genuine
  worker-restart notice, checking only git log/status and the dispatch PR's own
  comments is not enough to tell whether it made progress — it may already have
  filed a GitHub issue.** In issue #112, a subagent found a blocking finding and
  filed issue #113 moments before its worker restarted. The orchestrator's recovery
  check covered only git and PR-comment state (both clean, since the subagent's
  real output was a filed issue, not a commit), concluded "no progress survived,"
  and relaunched a second subagent from a from-scratch briefing — which
  re-investigated the same root cause and filed a duplicate, issue #114, wasting
  about 5m42s of redundant subagent work. Before asserting "no progress" in a
  relaunch briefing after a worker-restart, also search GitHub issues
  (`search_issues`/`list_issues`) for anything the lost subagent may have filed —
  not just the dispatch PR's own comments and local git log.
---VERSIONS.md---

{"number":277,"title":"converge-item.mjs can't run from a routine-fired Claude Code Web session (MCP-only GitHub access)","body":"## What happened

Executing work item #260 (`product-wiki/wiki-growth`), I reached `queue/instructions.md` step 6 — converge the issue in code:

```
node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs --issue 260 \
  --outcome done --summary '...' --pr 269
```

This is the mandated mechanism: the instructions say explicitly not to hand-perform the labeling/close/record steps the command does. It fails from this session for two stacked reasons:

1. **Without a proxy flag**, Node's built-in `fetch` (the default `fetchImpl` in `engine/scheduler/signals/gh.mjs`'s `makeGh()`) ignores `HTTPS_PROXY` entirely — a documented gap in `/root/.ccr/README.md`'s "Tool ignores the proxy entirely" section, whose fix is `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1` on Node ≥ 22.21. Without it, the request goes straight to `api.github.com` carrying the literal placeholder string `GITHUB_TOKEN` holds in this session, and GitHub itself returns a genuine `401`.
2. **With `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`** the request correctly routes through this session's egress proxy — but the proxy itself then denies it:
   ```
   403 {"message":"GitHub access is not enabled for this session. An org admin must connect the Claude GitHub App for this organization.", "documentation_url":"https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/github-actions"}
   ```

This session's own system prompt states plainly: *"You do NOT have access to the gh CLI, hub CLI, or direct GitHub API access. Instead, use the GitHub MCP server tools (prefixed with `mcp__github__`) for ALL GitHub interactions."* `converge-item.mjs` (via `signals/gh.mjs`'s `makeGh()`) is hard-wired to raw `fetch` + `process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN`, which is the Action-side credential shape — the file's own header comment even says so: *"engine/scheduler/ is the one place that legitimately uses the Action's GITHUB_TOKEN — everything session-side stays MCP-only."* Yet `queue/instructions.md` step 6 directs the **agentic session** (a Claude Code Web session fired by the queue's routine, per `queue/invoke.mjs`) to run this script directly.

## Why this looks like a real gap, not a one-off

`invoke.mjs`'s own comments confirm the agent hop is exactly a routine-fired Claude Code Web session — the same kind this run is. Checking recent closed work items in this repo (#259, #257, #242…), every one converged via `code-work` only ("Code-work did this run's work; no agent was needed") — none of them reached the agentic hand-off, so none exercised step 6's `converge-item.mjs` call from an actual agent session. This may be the first run in this repo to hit that path under the current queue model, which would explain why the mismatch hasn't surfaced before.

## Scope

I did **not** attempt to write a canon-side fix (no scratch canon clone in this session, and diagnosing the right fix — e.g. giving `converge-item.mjs` an MCP-backed transport, or changing what credential these routine-fired sessions carry — is a bigger call than this run's scope). Filing this as a repro so whoever owns the queue engine can decide the fix; work item #260 itself is left in its `task:agent`/open state rather than hand-converged, per `queue/instructions.md`'s own rule against performing that transition by hand.

## Verification

- `curl` to `api.github.com` for an out-of-scope repo: proxy `403` naming `add_repo`.
- `node` (no proxy flag) to `api.github.com` for **this** in-scope repo: real GitHub `401` (proxy bypassed).
- `node NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1` to `api.github.com` for this in-scope repo: proxy `403`, "GitHub access is not enabled for this session."
- The same session's MCP GitHub tools (`mcp__github__*`) worked throughout this run without issue (created/merged PR #269, created issues, added labels and comments).

{"number":54,"title":"resolve-dispatch exit 13 renders as a failed command when it is the normal handshake","body":"## What

Every CCR-triggered executor session runs `resolve-dispatch.mjs`, gets exit `13` (`needs-issue`), fetches the issue over MCP, and re-runs. That is the designed two-shot handshake — but a bare invocation surfaces in the session as a **failed** Bash call, so a normal run looks broken to anyone reading it.

## Decision

Keep the exit code. It is the machine interface the executor branches on, it is covered by `engine-tests/scheduler/resolve-dispatch.test.mjs`, and collapsing `13` to `0` would let the executor mistake "fetch the body and come back" for "you have a valid dispatch, go run it" — which is how the duplicate-execution bug gets back in.

Fix the *presentation* instead: `executor.md` invokes it with a trailing `echo "resolve-dispatch exit=$?"`, so the command succeeds and the verdict is printed for branching. Document in the shell that non-zero here is a verdict, not a fault (only `1`/`2` are faults).","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/54","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["needs-decision"],"assignees":[],"comments":10,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-01T06:00:21Z","updated_at":"2026-08-23T13:04:12Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":274,"title":"Canon defect: converge-item.mjs cannot run session-side — this session type has no direct GitHub API access","body":"Working item #240 (`claudinite-growth/growth-discover-packs`) ran to completion — findings logged on the tracker (#267) — but step 6 of `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/instructions.md` ("Converge the issue exactly once — in code, not by hand") could not execute.

### What happened

Following the instructions verbatim:

```
GITHUB_REPOSITORY=missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs \
  --issue 240 --outcome done --summary '...'
```

fails with `converge-item: #240 could not be read` — the underlying REST call to `/repos/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite/issues/240` returns `401 Bad credentials`. Not scoped to issue 240: `/repos/missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite` and `/rate_limit` fail the same way, with the same `GITHUB_TOKEN` this session's env carries.

Retrying with the session's outbound proxy actually engaged (`NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`, since Node's built-in `fetch` doesn't read `HTTPS_PROXY` on its own — see `/root/.ccr/README.md`) surfaces the real cause, as a structured 403 from the proxy itself:

> GitHub access is not enabled for this session. An org admin must connect the Claude GitHub App for this organization.

This session's GitHub access is MCP-only (`mcp__github__*` — used throughout this run, and used to post this issue) by explicit platform configuration for this deployment (a routine-fired "Claude Code on the web" session, per `engine/scheduler/queue/invoke.mjs`'s `agentInvoker`/`firePayload` — exactly the invocation path that started this session). Direct REST API / `gh` CLI access is a separate, disabled integration for this session type.

### Why this is a canon defect, not a one-off environment gap

`.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/signals/gh.mjs`'s own header comment says:

> `engine/scheduler/queue/` is the one place that legitimately uses the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` — **everything session-side stays MCP-only**.

But `converge-item.mjs` lives in `engine/scheduler/queue/` and is exactly what `instructions.md` §6 — the file that governs what a routine-fired session does — tells **the session itself** to run. That's a direct contradiction: the one script `instructions.md` hands the session for its mandatory terminal step depends on `gh.mjs`'s direct-REST client, which the engine's own comment says session-side code must not use. Every future work item that reaches an agent session through this exact flow (routine → Claude Code on the web) will hit the same wall at convergence, not just #240.

### What I did instead

Per `instructions.md`'s own guidance ("nothing below is yours to perform... doing it by hand anyway is how an item ends up closed wearing `task:agent`"), I did not hand-replicate the comment/label/close side effects via MCP. #240 is left open, still wearing `task:agent`/`agent:running` status, unconverged. Someone with the right scope needs to decide the fix — options that came to mind, not a prescription: give `converge-item.mjs` an MCP-backed `gh` implementation for session-side use (there's already a fake-`gh`-injectable seam per `gh.mjs`'s own doc comment), or have the Actions executor perform convergence itself once the session reports its outcome some other way. Either is an engine-side design call.

### Verification run

```
$ GITHUB_REPOSITORY=missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs --issue 240 --outcome done --summary '...'
converge-item: #240 could not be read   # underlying: 401 Bad credentials

$ GITHUB_REPOSITORY=missingbulb/ClaudiniteWebsite NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 node -e '...same call...'
403 {"message":"GitHub access is not enabled for this session. An org admin must connect the Claude GitHub App for this organization.", ...}
```

More importantly, the exit-1-on-unmatched-wake behavior this issue asks to soften is no longer just unhardened — it's now explicitly **intentional**, documented at `scheduler-run.mjs`'s wake-handling block: "A force that woke nothing is a failed force, and a green run saying so in a log line is how it goes unnoticed by the fleet lever that pressed it," and the code sets `process.exitCode = 1` on `unmatched.length` by design. That directly conflicts with this issue's ask (read here as "the tick script treats that as fatal rather than a no-op" being a bug to fix).

The narrow timing race this issue diagnosed (a `CLAUDINITE_WAKE` firing before its standing item exists) may still be real, but the fix isn't "make it a no-op" — that's the opposite of the current design's stated intent. Needs a human call: is the current design's philosophy right (loud failure on a failed force) and this issue should close, or does the timing race justify a narrower fix that doesn't undermine that intent? Relabeling `blocked` → `needs-decision`.

input.prompt:
You are helping with the "conversation half" of a Claudinite growth-extract pass on the repo /home/user/ClaudiniteWebsite. Your job is ONLY to read captured agent↔user session transcripts and report candidate durable lessons — you must NOT write any files or make any commits. This is pure research/reporting.

Read these three JSONL transcript files (each is a captured Claude Code session log — a sequence of JSON entries with timestamps, messages, tool_use/tool_result pairs):
- /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-ClaudiniteWebsite/dcf886fc-c649-5458-a725-ea4ffe86711e/scratchpad/logs/2026-08-13T2146Z--issue-157--a18774ee-1a3e-5b01-bf72-645353743ba8.jsonl
- /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-ClaudiniteWebsite/dcf886fc-c649-5458-a725-ea4ffe86711e/scratchpad/logs/2026-08-14T0317Z--issue-159--8aa24b53-d032-589a-9a59-e25c0e18c64c.jsonl
- /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-ClaudiniteWebsite/dcf886fc-c649-5458-a725-ea4ffe86711e/scratchpad/logs/2026-08-14T0516Z--issue-161--b98aafdc-f6ea-524a-9760-496b6ad1c576.jsonl

These are large (up to ~900KB) — use grep/sed/awk or partial reads to navigate efficiently rather than reading the whole file into context at once; look for structure like "role", "type":"tool_use"/"tool_result", timestamps, and text content fields.

## What to look for — friction signals

Read each conversation and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than necessary:

1. **Misunderstandings**: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an AskUserQuestion whose answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

2. **Suboptimal agent actions**: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant/repeated work; re-ran a command that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing convention and had it corrected in review.

3. **Long wall-time waits**: independent operations run serially that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a padded fixed sleep that over/undershot; a process waited out after its result was already in hand; blind long polling; re-running an already-green check. If you find one, MEASURE it with real timestamps from the log — quantify the wait in seconds/minutes, don't estimate.

4. **Recurring user questions**: does the user ask the same kind of question more than once across the session (e.g. "how many processes ran", "what took longest") that the agent could have answered proactively?

## The bar (don't over-report)

A signal is only worth reporting if the fix would be **durable, reusable, and generalizable** beyond this one session — not a one-off situational detail, not a generic truism, not something already obviously true. Do NOT report:
- The owner's own personal preferences (tone, which word triggers a merge, summary style) — these are injected per-person, not project rules.
- Agent-framework/harness loading mechanics (why a skill didn't mount, why an MCP tool wasn't available) — that's a platform bug to file upstream, not a project lesson.
- Anything about routing around a permission/security/classifier denial (a retry that succeeded) — never turn that into a "bypass and retry" rule.
- Anything already an obvious/generic best practice.

## Output format

For each candidate lesson, report:
- **Signal type** (1-4 above)
- **Evidence**: which file, approximate line/entry, a short quote or paraphrase (under ~50 words, don't dump raw transcript)
- **The proposed durable fix**: what future-facing rule, convention, or default would prevent this cost next time
- **Confidence**: high/medium/low that this clears the "durable and reusable" bar

If a log yields nothing durable, say so plainly and briefly — most logs yield nothing, that's expected and fine. Do not pad with marginal findings.

End your report with a short list of "no-comment" logs (yielded nothing) vs "candidate" logs (yielded at least one report-worthy signal).

Keep your final report under 1500 words total across all three logs.
